narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 66.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. By far the strongest influence was your third-year class ranking, which placed you in the bottom decile of your school. This was the single most important reason the model leaned toward predicting failure. Your first-year ranking also mattered, though less strongly; being in the fifth decile was somewhat below the average of accepted students and nudged the prediction slightly toward success, but not enough to offset later performance. Your LSAT score of 34 was the third most influential factor. While it pulled the prediction mildly toward passing, it still fell noticeably short of the 37.2 average among accepted applicants.

Taken together, these academic signals led the model to conclude that the risk of bar exam failure was too high for admission. Gender, race, family income bracket, undergraduate GPA, and planned full-time status played no role in the decision.

You should focus on strengthening your academic trajectory and retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving your class rank in future years and boosting your test performance would directly address the factors that most hurt your prediction and improve your chances in a future application.
